paragraphs.heading: Sorting things by probability
paragraphs.text: A naive Bayes classifier is a simple way to build a program that sorts things into categories, called classes, using probability. Each thing to be sorted is described by a list of feature values, and the program picks its label from a fixed, finite set of classes. What makes it naive Bayes is one assumption: once you know the class, the features are treated as independent of each other. Put another way, each feature is taken to say something about the class on its own, sharing nothing with what the other features say.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: That assumption is wildly unrealistic, and that is exactly why the method is called naive. Picture a fruit judged to be an apple because it is red, round and about 10 cm across. The classifier lets each of those three clues push the chance of apple up or down by itself. It ignores any way that colour, roundness and size might tend to go together.

paragraphs.heading: Why it still works
paragraphs.text: Even with such a crude design, these classifiers have done quite well on many complex real-world problems. A 2004 analysis found sound theoretical reasons for this surprising success. Still, a broad comparison in 2006 showed that other approaches, such as boosted trees or random forests, beat it. It also usually does worse than more advanced models like logistic regression at saying how sure it is, and its probabilities are often wildly overconfident.

paragraphs.heading: Cheap and quick to train
paragraphs.text: One strength is that it scales easily: it needs just one parameter for each feature. Training with the method called maximum likelihood comes down to a direct formula, which in practice means counting how often things happen in each group. Most other models instead need expensive algorithms that creep toward an answer step by step. It also needs only a small amount of training data to estimate what it needs.

paragraphs.heading: Bayes in name only
paragraphs.text: The method uses Bayes' theorem when it makes a decision, but it is not necessarily a Bayesian method. It can be fitted to data using either Bayesian or frequentist methods. In many practical uses it is fitted by maximum likelihood, so you can work with it without accepting Bayesian probability at all.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting documents and spam
paragraphs.text: For features that come in separate categories, as in sorting documents or filtering spam, two kinds of model are popular. In the multinomial version, each document becomes a tally, counting how many times each word turns up in it. In the Bernoulli version, each feature is a simple yes or no, recording only whether a term appears.

paragraphs.heading: The problem with zero
paragraphs.text: Counting has a trap. If some class and some feature value never appear together in the training data, the estimated probability for that pair comes out as zero. Because the probabilities are multiplied together, that single zero wipes out everything the other features said. A common fix is to add a small extra count, called a pseudocount, to every estimate so that nothing is ever exactly zero; with a pseudocount of one this is called Laplace smoothing, and in general Lidstone smoothing.
